# Preface {.unnumbered}

This book provides a progressive introduction to the finite element method, with
an emphasis on understanding how the method is formulated, implemented, and
verified.

The mechanical development begins by contrasting continuous and discrete
systems. We then use simple spring assemblies, which can be solved and verified
by hand, to introduce the direct stiffness method and its fundamental algebraic
ingredients. Later, these same principles are extended to finite element
discretizations of continuum problems.

Theory and computation are developed together. Julia is used because its syntax
stays close to mathematical notation while still delivering high performance.
The exposition is tightly coordinated with successive versions of the
accompanying pedagogical code, MiniFEM.

The primary target audience is students with an engineering background and a
basic knowledge of solid or structural mechanics and of numerical analysis,
although the material may also be useful to students from related disciplines.

Finite element concepts are developed through computational examples of
increasing generality, with the aim of connecting mathematical formulations,
numerical algorithms, and their software implementation. Throughout the book,
particular attention is given to verification and to the interpretation of
numerical results.

This book is built with [Quarto](https://quarto.org/docs/books).

OpenAI's ChatGPT was used to support language editing, structural revision, and
the review of selected explanations and code examples. The author remains fully
responsible for the technical content and final editorial decisions.

# About MiniFEM {.unnumbered}

MiniFEM is a pedagogical finite element code written in Julia and developed
alongside the material presented in this book. Its source code and successive
development snapshots are hosted in the
[`MiniFEM.jl`](https://github.com/angelosimone/MiniFEM.jl) repository.

Its development begins with self-contained scripts that closely mirror hand
calculations and proceeds toward increasingly structured and modular
implementations. The purpose of MiniFEM is to make the essential components of a
finite element implementation explicit and directly inspectable.

At a later stage, the presentation transitions to established Julia finite
element libraries such as
[`Ferrite.jl`](https://ferrite-fem.github.io/Ferrite.jl/stable/). The concepts
developed through MiniFEM provide the basis for understanding the more general
abstractions and workflows introduced by these libraries.

The chapters of the book are coordinated with successive snapshots of the
`MiniFEM.jl` repository. Early snapshots document the progressive development of
MiniFEM, while later ones include examples and applications based on
`Ferrite.jl`. Each snapshot captures a particular stage in the development of
the course material.
